name: Treaty with the Potawatomi, October 26, 1832 (Treaty of Tippecanoe)
nations: Potawatomi of Indiana, today including the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, Pokagon Band, Forest County Potawatomi, Hannahville Indian Community, Match-e-be-nash-she-wish Band and Nottawaseppi Huron Band
promises: Article 1: the Potawatomi ceded their land in northwestern Indiana between Lake Michigan, the Illinois line and earlier cession lines (Royce Area 180).

Article 2: reservations were kept for named bands, including thirty-six sections for Aub-be-naub-bee's band and twenty-two sections for the bands of Menominee, No-taw-kah, Muck-kah-tah-mo-way and Pee-pin-oh-waw.
Article 3: an annuity of $20,000 for twenty years, $100,000 in goods, and a further $30,000 in goods in 1833.
Articles 4 to 6: payment of $62,412 in listed debts, help equal to that given other emigrating tribes if the Potawatomi chose to move, and a sawmill.

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found that the United States paid $453,698.00 under this treaty for the Potawatomi interest in Royce Area 180, plus $128,856.60 in food and provisions, a combined $582,554.60, for land with a fair market value of $2,440,941.85, and that the consideration was unconscionable.

breaches.quote: so grossly inadequate as to render the consideration unconscionable

breaches.what: The Commission's order setting awards gave the Potawatomi plaintiffs a total of $4,497,815.59 in additional compensation for four cessions together, one of them the October 26, 1832 cession of Royce Area 180, subject to any gratuitous offsets.

breaches.what: The chiefs of the 22-section reserve kept for them in Article 2 protested that the treaty of August 5, 1836 sold that reserve without their knowledge or consent, that none of their bands except two unauthorised men signed it, and that names appearing on any paper were put there falsely.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Menominee, Muck-kah-tah-mo-way, Pee-pin-oh-waw and the son of No-taw-kah, chiefs named in the 1832 treaty, letter of protest to Secretary of War Lewis Cass, November 15, 1836

source.title: Menominee's letters of protest, 1836-1837 (transcribed from National Archives microfilm M234, roll 355; Wayback capture of January 4, 2024)

compensation: The Commission's 1978 award of $4,497,815.59 to the Potawatomi covers the 1826, 1828 and both October 1832 cessions together; the share for this treaty alone is not stated in the order opened, and gratuitous offsets were still to be decided.
today: The later fate of the Article 2 band reservations, and the removal of Menominee's band from Indiana in 1838 (the Trail of Death), were not traced to a finding in this pass.

openQuestions: The OSU collection dates the opinion September 28, 1978 and the order setting awards September 8, 1978; both are 43 Ind. Cl. Comm. 74. The order's own text says it was dated the 8th day of September 1978, which is used here.
The 1978 case was later transferred to the Court of Claims (order of September 29, 1978 in a related docket); the final paid amount was not found.

treaties.json attaches eight Royce cessions (180, 200, 209, 210, 218, 325, 436, 437) to this id; only 180 belongs to this treaty, the others are later cessions of the reserved lands and of Kansas lands. Worth correcting in treaties.json.

Whether the reserved band lands of Article 2 were later ceded without the bands' consent (Menominee's refusal of the 1836 Yellow River treaty) was not traced to a finding. No nation statement was found in this pass.

nationVoice.nation: Potawatomi of the Yellow River reserve (Chief Menominee and the chiefs named in this treaty)
nationVoice.summary: In letters of protest to the Secretary of War (November 15, 1836) and President Jackson (April 6, 1837), Menominee and the other chiefs recognised by the Treaty of Tippecanoe say the August 1836 treaty selling their 22-section reserve was a false treaty made without their knowledge or consent, signed only by two men with no authority, and ask that it be rejected so they may stay on their land.
